title: Cold calling at top of Mulino’s super hit list
full_text:
The federal government is finalising reforms to protect Australians from dodgy superannuation operators, with a ban on lead generation now expected in the wake of a $1bn super investment scandal.
Alongside the crackdown on lead generation, also known as cold calling, an ill-designed compensation scheme for victims of financial misconduct is set to be overhauled, as self-managed super funds brace to be tapped to help pay for the controversial scheme.
In his first National Press Club address later this month, Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is also expected to follow through on the government’s proposal that super trustees be forced to cover investor losses in the case of fraud.
But measures making it harder for Australians to switch super funds, including introducing waiting periods for moving between funds, are not expected to make it onto the final hit list.
“Ensuring Australians having confidence in their retirement, and in our superannuation system, is a non-negotiable for this government,” a government spokesperson said in response to The Australian’s questions about the looming reforms.
“All Australians deserve a dignified retirement, and it is essential that our investment and superannuation systems remain robust,” the spokesperson said.
“At his first National Press Club address, the Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services, Daniel Mulino, will address the importance of superannuation for all Australians and what the Albanese government is doing to protect consumers and their superannuation in an evolving financial system.”
The reforms, to be announced on August 19, are the government’s solution to plugging the gaping holes that led to the collapse of two investment schemes, the Shield Master Fund and the First Guardian Master Fund. They are the result of months of consultation with regulators, industry and consumer groups.
Shield and First Guardian were two failed managed investment schemes that grew at a rapid clip over a few years due to high-pressure sales tactics. Both funds are now in liquidation and under investigation by the corporate cop, having cost more than 11,000 Australians up to $1bn in super savings.
The scandal exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia’s $4.5 trillion retirement nest egg, with alleged failures all along the investment chain, from the ratings houses to the advisers, the super trustees and the funds themselves.
After consulting with regulators, industry and consumer advocates, the government is understood to be leaning toward an outright ban of lead generation in super.
The other option being weighed is forcing lead generators to be licensed, like financial advisers. But licensed advisers were at the centre of the Shield and First Guardian collapses, with critics arguing licensing the operators doesn’t go far enough.
Dr Mulino is also expected to announce changes to the widely panned Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, including removing the controversial ‘but for’ provision that sees victims of financial misconduct compensated for hypothetical losses.
The CSLR hands up to $150,000 in compensation to victims of financial misconduct when the responsible firm is insolvent.
It is an industry-funded scheme that has been in strife since its launch just a couple of years ago due to a series of financial advice scandals, including Dixon Advisory, United Global Capital, First Guardian and Shield. It has already paid more than $200m to victims of financial conduct in just two years.
If, as expected, the government removes the ‘but for’ provision, victims will only be entitled to actual losses, up to the $150,000 limit.
As well, Dr Mulino is expected to bring SMSFs into the CSLR funding umbrella as the scheme faces a shortfall of $170m for the 2027 financial year. A special levy will apply to parts of the sector, including SMSFs and APRA-regulated funds, as well as others.
The SMSF Association has argued any levy, if it applies to the self-managed part of the sector, should be only temporary and “very small”. Chief executive Peter Burgess recently estimated it may end up being roughly $60 per SMSF this year.
“We don’t want this to be every year. This should only be applied to get us out of the situation we’re in at the moment where we have this massive shortfall. Hopefully, the changes the government is looking at making to the CSLR means we won’t need special levies going forward,” Mr Burgess said.
